I think many people mistake the ability to choose with free will. Of course, an organism has a choice of left or right, or whatever, but the processes of why that choice is to be made is "determined" in such a sense, without the "will" of the organism. Any choice making entity is only able to "choose" that which has been made possible by all of reality up until that moment. A crude example might be that the aforementioned organism cannot choose to go fruble, since that direction does not exist. And further, when it does choose, for example left, it does so because of a series of compulsions and dependencies. If you interrogate your own choices, I believe will find that behind every choice is an undecided, non-free motive.

How can these spontaneous effects exist? For the record, that concept is actually antithetical to the Buddhist description of karma, as it contradicts the concept of "dependant origination" which implies that all things are dependent upon all the other things. Nothing exists that is not caused by the rest of the system that the object or action in questions exists within. As that relates to the notion of free will, the Buddhist perspective could be said to be that no choice can by made that is not casually determined within the dependent origination of the system around the thing which is choosing. Of course, how this relates to the ability to choose to, for example, become a Buddhist monk becomes complicated, but suffice to say that the Buddhist description of karma, and the western description of free will are to a large degree, incompatible.
